summary.text: 穿 means to bore or pierce through. A traditional explanation pictures a tooth inside a hole; a competing account proposes that an early spelling included a sound element, but its reading and graphic history remain disputed.

formation.text: The traditional analysis treats 穿 as an ideographic compound: 穴 is a hole and 牙 is a tooth shown within it, together suggesting penetration. A competing analysis proposes that an early spelling had a sound-bearing element written with 耳 and 串, later altered through confusion between 耳 and 牙. That reading and sequence remain disputed; available comparisons do not establish a phonetic role for 穴 or 牙.

components.text: In the traditional explanation, 穴 depicts the hole containing the tooth and contributes the setting for penetration. No sound comparison establishes a phonetic role for it.

In the traditional explanation, 牙 depicts the tooth within the hole. A competing account proposes that this visible form reflects confusion with an earlier 耳, but that graphic change remains disputed; no sound comparison establishes 牙 as phonetic.

history.text: The received traditional account explains 穿 as 牙 inside 穴 and glosses it as passage or penetration. This is a historical explanation of the graph, not independent confirmation of its original motivation.

A character catalogue lists Chu manuscript and small-seal examples, but the images could not be inspected. It lists no oracle-bone or bronze forms; that is a limit of the catalogue consulted, not proof that such forms do not exist.

A specialist discussion reports a Chu manuscript spelling with 耳 and 串 in the Shijing passage and proposes a path to 穿 involving a sound element and later graphic confusion between 耳 and 牙. The spelling’s reading as 穿, 貫, or a form related to 聯, and the proposed graphic history, remain disputed.

uncertainties.text: The traditional tooth-in-hole explanation is documented, while the proposed Chu spelling and its phonetic reanalysis remain unresolved. No same-system historical sound comparison for 穴 or 牙 is available here, so neither is assigned a phonetic role.

The Chu spelling’s reading as 穿, 貫, or a form related to 聯 is unsettled. The catalogue lists early forms, but the images could not be inspected, and the evidence does not establish an earlier graphic sequence.

senses.period: pre-Qin Shijing corpus; exact composition date unresolved
senses.text: The earliest textual use located is in the Shijing passage Xing Lu, where 穿 describes boring through a house or wall. This attests the word in that text, though the poem’s precise composition date is unresolved.
Historical sources attest uses meaning “pass through.” They do not establish a precise development from the piercing sense.
Texts attest uses for threading or joining, but do not show when or by what steps these uses developed from “pierce through.”

senses.gloss: dig or excavate, including a canal
senses.text: Historical sources attest digging, including digging a canal. They do not establish a semantic path connecting these uses to the piercing sense.
Later texts attest the clothing and footwear sense. Its precise development from the older senses is not established.
Sources separately attest a worn or broken sense, but do not show how it developed from the other senses.

limitations.text: Several historical senses are attested, but their chronology and semantic transitions are not established. The earliest use located is in the Shijing corpus, whose exact composition date is unresolved.

evidence.source: 《漢語多功能字庫》, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The entry lists a seal-script form and six Chu bamboo-and-silk forms for 穿, but no oracle-bone or bronze examples. evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 穿

evidence.source: 《說文解字》 online text and 段玉裁 commentary
evidence.text: The received Shuowen entry glosses 穿 as “通也” and explains its form as a tooth (牙) inside a cave or hole (穴). Duan Yucai quotes the Shijing line about a mouse boring through a wall. This is an early lexicographic analysis, not independent confirmation of the original graphic motivation.
evidence.title: 說文解字「穿」

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry cites the Shijing, Shao Nan, Xing Lu line “誰謂鼠無牙，何以穿我墉？” for the sense “pierce through.” It separately cites Huainanzi for threading or passing through, Han shu for digging a canal, Tang poetry and later texts for wearing clothes, and Gongyang zhuan for worn or broken. These citations document distinct uses; the list itself does not establish when or by what steps one sense developed from another.
evidence.title: A02957 穿 — 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Chinese Text Project, Book of Poetry
evidence.text: The Xing Lu text contains both “何以穿我屋” and “何以穿我墉,” in a context where 穿 means bore through a house or wall. This is the earliest textual use located in this research; the poem is conventionally assigned to the pre-Qin Shijing corpus, but this source page does not date the composition more precisely.
evidence.title: 詩經: 國風: 召南: 行露

evidence.source: Chinese Text Project, dictionary entry for 穿
evidence.text: The entry records meanings and examples including digging, passing through, threading or joining, a hole, a grave, a watercourse, a tea vessel, and worn or broken. It also supplies examples from texts such as Liji, Lunheng, Han shu, Shuijing zhu, and Gongyang zhuan. These attestations show a broader historical range, but do not by themselves establish a chronological chain from the piercing sense to each later sense.
evidence.title: 穿 — 中國哲學書電子化計劃

evidence.source: Pan Deng, discussion of the Anda University Chu manuscript Shijing, citing the 2019 manuscript edition and other scholarship
evidence.text: The discussion reports an Anda Chu manuscript form in the Xing Lu passage with an 耳 component and 串 sound element, corresponding to received 穿. The author argues that this spelling records the word 穿 and proposes that Qin-Han graphic change, including confusion between 耳 and 牙, produced the familiar 穿 shape from a form written with 穴 and a reduced sound element. Another cited interpretation reads related Chu examples as 貫 or connects the form with 聯. This is a disputed paleographic argument reported in a specialist discussion, not a settled account; the source’s glyph images were not visually inspected.
evidence.title: 安大簡《詩經》初讀 — 简帛网

evidence.source: Japanese Wiktionary, 穿 entry
evidence.text: This entry presents a phonetic analysis: 穴 plus a reduced form associated with an 耳-plus-串 spelling, later altered by graphic confusion between 耳 and 牙. It gives 穿 Mandarin chuān, Middle Chinese tsyhwen, and Old Chinese *tʰon {*tʰo[n]}. The analysis points to 布之道’s 廣韻形聲考, but that cited page was not accessible in this research, so the etymological chain lacks direct verification here. The entry is secondary and its proposed analysis remains disputed.
evidence.title: 穿 — ウィクショナリー日本語版

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database gives modern Mandarin chuān and Middle Chinese fanqie 昌緣切 for the level-tone reading and 尺絹 for a departing-tone reading; the associated Guangyun categories are third-division rounded Xian and Xian departing tone. These support the character’s readings but do not alone establish the pronunciation of an alleged phonetic component.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 穿

evidence.source: Pan Deng, discussion of Anda manuscript evidence and phonological interpretation
evidence.text: The discussion compares reconstructed Old Chinese forms for 穿 and 貫 and describes the Chu manuscript spelling’s 串 element as phonetically related, while noting that the consonant relationship may appear distant under conventional initials. It advances a “special 昌 initial” account and treats 穿 and 貫 as related in sound and possibly cognate. This is the discussant’s analysis, not an independently confirmed reconstruction. No specific pronunciation for 穴 or 牙 is offered as support for their being sound components.
evidence.title: 安大簡《詩經》初讀 — 简帛网

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No oracle-bone or bronze attestation for 穿 was found in inspected character references; this is a limit of consulted sources, not proof that none exists.

The Shuowen component explanation and modern proposal of a phonetic spelling with 耳/串 elements conflict. The latter is only partially supported by a specialist discussion; its main cited monograph page could not be accessed.
Whether the disputed Chu manuscript graph should be read as 穿, 貫, or connected historically to 聯 remains unsettled in the inspected evidence.
No visually inspected glyph images were used; graphic descriptions here are source reports.

The six Chu manuscript forms reported by the CUHK database are not individually dated or reproduced in accessible text. The earliest textual attestation located is the pre-Qin Shijing corpus, but its composition date is not established precisely here.

Modern 穴 and 牙 readings and same-system historical reconstructions were not recovered from an accessible primary phonological database result. Therefore no phonetic role for either component is established on sound comparison in this report; the whole character’s proposed phonetic reanalysis remains disputed.

Later senses such as threading, passage, wearing, holes, graves, waterways, vessels, and worn/broken are textually attested in later sources, but a precise chronology or semantic derivation for every sense is not demonstrated by gloss order.
The source references inspected here provide no oracle-bone or bronze forms for 穿. This is a limit of the consulted entry, not proof none exist.

Shuowen’s tooth-in-hole analysis is a received historical explanation. The dossier’s competing Chu-script account involving an 耳/串 spelling and later confusion is not independently resolved by the pages successfully inspected in this invocation.

The early disputed manuscript reading (穿, 貫, or a graph associated with 聯) and the proposed phonetic reassignment remain uncertain. The cited specialist discussion in the dossier is not new verification in this invocation.

No component-specific modern and same-system historical pronunciation comparison for 穴 and 牙 was established. The available entry gives readings for 穿 but does not show evidence that either component functions phonetically; the semantic-component account is supported as a source assertion, while the alternative remains unverified here.

The earliest text located in the dossier is the received pre-Qin Shijing corpus; the poem’s precise composition date is not established by the pages inspected here. Later dictionary citations attest senses separately but do not establish each semantic bridge or chronology.

No historical glyph image candidate met the requirement for verified identity, inspectable description, direct image URL, and reuse provenance. The CUHK linked images were inaccessible or empty; Commons searches/open attempts failed to establish a 穿 file. The text-only form catalogue provides no image reuse rights.

limitations.text: No candidate image could be selected: the available research does not establish a verifiable, inspectable glyph image of 穿 with reusable rights. The listed seal and Chu manuscript forms could not be inspected, so their visible features and individual identities remain unconfirmed.
